title: Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation Asks Biden to Sanction 35 Russians
description_medium: In January 2021, Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation asked President Joe Biden to sanction 35 Russian officials and business figures it associated with corruption, repression, and Navalny’s persecution. The foundation highlighted eight people as priorities; seven of the 35 were already under U.S. sanctions. This was an advocacy request to the Biden administration, not a Trump action.
description_long: Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation sent the Biden administration a list of 35 Russian officials and business figures it wanted sanctioned. The request followed Navalny’s return to Russia on January 17, 2021, and his subsequent detention. The foundation said the people on its list were connected to corruption, suppression of civil and political freedoms, or the persecution of Navalny and his organization. It identified eight names as a priority shortlist; seven of the full 35 were already subject to U.S. sanctions. The request was directed to President Joe Biden after he took office and asked for new executive action. It was not itself a sanctions decision, and the description should preserve the foundation’s allegations as allegations. The request was directed to President Joe Biden after he took office, asking the new administration to consider further sanctions in response to Navalny’s detention.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Anti-Corruption Foundation asks Biden to sanction 35 Russians
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation Asks Biden to Sanction 35 Russians
corrected_wording.reason: This was an advocacy request to the Biden administration, with no established direct Trump action.

source_access_notes: The supplied timeline attributes the allegations to Navalny’s foundation; CNN coverage is linked in the record for the request.
blockers: This January 2021 advocacy request was directed to President Biden; the supplied evidence establishes no direct Trump action or connection beyond cross-references to other timeline entries.
rationale: Describes the foundation’s Biden-era sanctions request and makes clear the record does not document a Trump action.

title: Bukele Offers to House Convicted U.S. Citizens in Salvadoran Prisons
description_medium: During Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s February 2025 visit, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to house deportees from the United States in Salvadoran prisons. Rubio said the offer extended to U.S. citizens and legal residents convicted of violent crimes, though it was unclear whether the United States would accept it. No American was transferred under the proposal.
description_long: During a February 3, 2025 meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to house people deported from the United States in Salvadoran prisons. Rubio said the offer included people of any nationality and also U.S. citizens or legal residents already convicted of violent crimes and serving sentences. Bukele described the proposal as outsourcing part of El Salvador’s prison system for a fee and referred to the country’s high-security Terrorism Confinement Center. The next day, Rubio said the administration would study the offer’s legality; President Trump said he would pursue it if he had legal authority. Reuters reported that U.S. citizens cannot legally be deported, and the administration had not decided whether to accept Bukele’s offer. The statements documented a proposal and its political discussion, not a completed transfer arrangement or an American sent to CECOT. The offer remained under study, and no transfer arrangement involving U.S. citizens was announced.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: U.S. makes deal to deport Americans to El Salvador terrorist prison
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Bukele Offers to House Convicted U.S. Citizens in Salvadoran Prisons
corrected_wording.reason: The documented event is a public offer discussed by Rubio, not a signed transfer agreement or a deportation of U.S. citizens.

source_access_notes: Reuters and AP report Bukele’s public offer, Rubio’s description, and the administration’s stated need to review legality.
rationale: Replaces the completed-deal framing with the documented public offer and separates U.S. citizens from deportable noncitizens.

title: Project 2025 Proposes Greater Federal Influence Over Criminal Justice
description_medium: Project 2025’s Mandate for Leadership recommended stronger White House supervision of the Justice Department and changes to federal enforcement and prosecution. The Brennan Center argued that these proposals could weaken prosecutorial independence and extend federal influence over local law enforcement.
description_long: Project 2025’s Mandate for Leadership is a policy blueprint published by the Heritage Foundation before the 2024 election. Its criminal-justice recommendations included stronger White House oversight of the Justice Department, changes to federal prosecutorial priorities, and a larger federal role in responding to local law-enforcement policies. The Brennan Center for Justice argued that these proposals could weaken norms protecting prosecutorial independence and expand presidential influence over law enforcement. Its analysis focused on how the recommendations might affect the separation between political leadership and federal prosecutions if adopted. The blueprint proposed changes to government structure and enforcement priorities; it was not itself an executive order or a completed policy action.

corrected_wording.original_title: Permanent Federal Power and Suppression of Political Opposition
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Project 2025 Proposes Greater Federal Influence Over Criminal Justice
corrected_wording.reason: The linked sources describe policy proposals and analysis, not a finalized Trump declaration or the alleged arrests, protest bans, citizenship revocations, and opposition eradication.

source_access_notes: The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 blueprint and the Brennan Center analysis were reviewed; both concern proposals and projected implications.
blockers: The cited analysis discusses potential effects of Project 2025 recommendations; it does not document arrests, protest bans, citizenship revocations, or elimination of political organizations.
rationale: Limits the entry to the documented policy recommendations and the Brennan Center’s attributed analysis; unsupported allegations about completed repression remain a blocker.

title: Trump Directs Review of Smithsonian and Federal Historical Displays
description_medium: On March 27, 2025, Trump signed the executive order “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” It criticized Smithsonian exhibits for what the order called divisive, race-centered ideology and directed the vice president to review exhibitions, with potential elimination of content it deemed inconsistent with the administration’s view of American history.
description_long: On March 27, 2025, Trump signed the executive order “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” It criticized Smithsonian exhibits for what it called divisive, race-centered ideology and singled out “The Shape of Power: Stories of Race and American Sculpture,” an exhibition on race in U.S. history. The order directed the vice president to review Smithsonian exhibitions and contemplated removing content the administration considered inconsistent with its stated approach to American history. It also instructed the Interior Department to review monuments and memorials and restore some that had been removed or altered since 2020. The order established a review process affecting federal historical presentation. Its broad standards left officials substantial discretion in evaluating exhibits and public monuments. The event was an executive directive about oversight and review, not a documented removal of the named exhibit.

corrected_wording.corrected_title: Trump Directs Review of Smithsonian and Federal Historical Displays
corrected_wording.reason: Corrects the overbroad removal claim to the order’s documented review directive.

source_access_notes: The cited source covers the event described.
blockers: The order establishes review authority and possible future changes, but no removal of the named exhibition is documented in this entry.
rationale: Describes the order’s review directives and the exhibit it named; a completed removal is not established.

title: NLRB Pauses SpaceX Worker Case as Settlement Talks Begin
description_medium: In April 2025, the National Labor Relations Board paused proceedings in a case alleging SpaceX fired employees for criticizing Elon Musk while the agency pursued settlement discussions. The move put the litigation on hold but did not itself decide whether the workers were unlawfully fired or establish settlement terms.
description_long: The National Labor Relations Board’s general counsel moved to pause an unfair-labor-practice case involving SpaceX while seeking settlement talks. The complaint alleged that the company unlawfully fired employees after they circulated an open letter criticizing Elon Musk and workplace conditions. SpaceX separately challenged the Board’s authority in federal court, leaving the labor case and the constitutional litigation on parallel tracks. The April 2025 move changed the immediate handling of the administrative complaint while settlement discussions began. It did not determine whether the firings violated labor law. The filing concerned workers’ protected activity and the Board’s authority to pursue the case, making the pause significant to both the employees’ claims and the agency’s enforcement process. At the time of the reported pause, no settlement terms or final decision on the allegations had been announced.

corrected_wording.corrected_title: NLRB Pauses SpaceX Worker Case as Settlement Talks Begin
corrected_wording.reason: The account supports a pause and settlement discussions but gives no terms or final disposition; the title’s “rids itself” implies a completed dismissal.

source_access_notes: The cited source covers the event described.
blockers: The account supports a pause and settlement discussions but gives no terms or final disposition; the title’s “rids itself” implies a completed dismissal.
rationale: Describes the pause, settlement effort and underlying allegations; no final settlement or determination was reported at that stage.

title: U.S. Approves UAE Arms Sales; RTX and Emirates Global Aluminum Announce Cooperation
description_medium: During Trump’s May 2025 Gulf visit, the State Department notified Congress of proposed arms sales to the UAE valued at about $1.45 billion. Trump also announced a cooperation memorandum between defense company RTX and Emirates Global Aluminum. The sales and the corporate memorandum were separate developments.
description_long: During Trump’s May 2025 visit to the United Arab Emirates, the State Department notified Congress of proposed arms sales worth about $1.45 billion. The proposal included six CH-47F Block II Chinook helicopters and related support equipment. Separately, Trump announced that U.S. defense company RTX and Emirates Global Aluminum had signed a memorandum of understanding to cooperate. One announcement concerned a proposed U.S. government arms sale; the other was a corporate partnership announcement. They were not a single intergovernmental defense package. The two developments accompanied the state visit and reflected separate government and business ties between the countries.

title: Trump Visits Qatar as Qatar Airways Announces Boeing Jet Order
description_medium: During Trump’s May 14, 2025 visit to Qatar, Qatar Airways agreed to buy up to 210 Boeing aircraft with GE Aerospace engines. Qatar also offered a Boeing 747-8 for temporary use as Air Force One while replacement aircraft were being completed. The offer raised questions about accepting a high-value gift from a foreign government.
description_long: Trump’s May 14, 2025 visit to Doha coincided with a signing ceremony for U.S.-Qatar agreements and Qatar Airways’ agreement to buy up to 210 Boeing aircraft with GE Aerospace engines. Separately, Qatar had offered a Boeing 747-8 for use as Air Force One while Boeing completed replacement aircraft. Trump defended the offer as a cost-saving measure and said the plane would be transferred to a government entity. The aircraft purchase involved a state-owned airline and U.S. manufacturers; the proposed government gift involved a separate transfer of an expensive aircraft for presidential use. Their timing brought commercial diplomacy and questions about foreign gifts into the same public discussion. The visit included defense and economic cooperation, while the aircraft offer raised questions about the terms and oversight of accepting valuable foreign-government property.

title: White House Loses Confidence in Hegseth Pentagon Leak Inquiry
description_medium: A May 2025 Guardian report said White House advisers lost confidence in a Pentagon leak inquiry overseen by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore. Advisers doubted a claim that a warrantless NSA wiretap had identified aides accused of leaking information. The dispute followed Hegseth’s firing of three senior aides.
description_long: White House advisers lost confidence in a Pentagon leak investigation after being told that a warrantless National Security Agency wiretap had identified aides accused of leaking information. The Guardian reported that advisers believed the wiretap account was false and were troubled by information from Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, who had been overseeing the inquiry. The investigation followed Hegseth’s firing of three senior aides the previous month. The disputed surveillance claim became a point of tension between the White House and Pentagon over how the dismissals had been justified. The report describes the advisers’ reaction and the breakdown in confidence around the inquiry. It does not provide a final investigative finding about the leaks or an independently verified account of the claimed surveillance.

corrected_wording.corrected_title: White House Loses Confidence in Hegseth Pentagon Leak Inquiry

source_access_notes: The cited source covers the event described.
blockers: The Guardian reports advisers’ doubts about the surveillance claim but does not provide independent confirmation of the claim or a final investigative finding.
rationale: Keeps the reader description on the reported loss of confidence and the underlying inquiry; the headline’s allegation of deliberate lying remains unsubstantiated.

title: State Department Cuts Analysts Who Modeled Strait of Hormuz Disruptions
description_medium: The State Department laid off energy analysts in July 2025 whose work included modeling a possible closure of the Strait of Hormuz, according to NOTUS. The strait carries a substantial share of global oil shipments. The layoffs occurred months before the 2026 Iran conflict; the evidence does not show that the staffing cuts changed U.S. planning or response.
description_long: NOTUS reported that the State Department laid off employees in July 2025 who had handled analysis of Middle Eastern oil and gas crises, including scenarios in which the Strait of Hormuz was blocked. The strait is a major shipping route for global oil supplies, so contingency planning for a closure bears on energy security and crisis response. Staff remaining at other agencies told NOTUS that the transition of this work did not occur after the State Department analysts were dismissed. The report situates the cuts within the Trump administration’s reduction-in-force initiative.

corrected_wording.corrected_title: State Department Cuts Analysts Who Modeled Strait of Hormuz Disruptions

source_access_notes: The cited source covers the event described.
blockers: NOTUS dates the layoffs to July 2025 but does not identify the number of analysts or demonstrate how the staffing reduction affected later U.S. response planning.
rationale: Uses the corrected July layoff timing and reported analyst role; the title’s comparison to later strikes and asserted operational effect are not established.

title: Trump Appoints Former Lawyer Will Scharf to Lead Federal Planning Commission
description_medium: On July 9, 2025, Trump appointed White House staff secretary Will Scharf, a former personal lawyer, to chair the National Capital Planning Commission. He also named Michael Blair and Stuart Levenbach as commissioners. The commission reviews federal development and planning in the Washington region.
description_long: President Donald Trump appointed Will Scharf to chair the National Capital Planning Commission in July 2025. Scharf was serving as White House staff secretary and had previously represented Trump as a personal lawyer. Trump also appointed Michael Blair, representing Virginia, and Stuart Levenbach, representing Maryland. The commission reviews federal plans and development in the National Capital Region, including federal buildings, memorials, parks and major changes to federal property. In introductory remarks, Scharf acknowledged that he had no direct background in architecture or urban planning. The appointment placed a senior White House aide at the head of a body that reviews plans affecting the capital region’s built environment and public spaces. The commission’s planning work includes evaluating projects for their relationship to the city’s comprehensive plan and federal interests in the region.
